summary: Early on the first day, an angel of the Lord rolls back the stone in a great earthquake and sits on it; the guards become like dead men.
key_insight: Matthew never describes Jesus leaving the tomb. The angel rolled back the stone and sat on it, the very stone the authorities had sealed. The men posted to guard a dead body “became like dead men.”
story: Early on the first day of the week, “there was a great earthquake; for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and came and rolled back the stone from the door, and sat on it.”
“His countenance was like lightning, and his clothing as white as snow.”
The guards shook for fear of him and became like dead men.

fit.question: Matthew tells of the earthquake right after the women set out for the tomb (28:1). Mark and Luke say the women found the stone already rolled away. Did the women see the angel move it?

points.label: Matthew does not place them there
points.text: Matthew says the women came “as the first day of the week began to dawn.” Then he tells what happened at the tomb, but he never says the women were present when the stone moved. The guards saw it, and some of them later reported it (28:11).

points.label: Finishing the guard’s story
points.text: Matthew has followed the guard since 27:62. He finishes that thread before turning back to the women, as a storyteller completes one scene before picking up another.

fit.note: Matthew tells what happened at the tomb; Mark and Luke tell what the women found when they arrived. The accounts fit together.
fit.short: Matthew never says the women saw the stone move; the guards witnessed it, and the women arrived to find it rolled away.

scene.label: An angel of the Lord
scene.text: Matthew used the same phrase at the start of his Gospel, when an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in dreams (1:20; 2:13, 19). The language that opened the story of Jesus’ birth now opens the story of His resurrection.

scene.label: Earthquakes
scene.text: Matthew alone records two earthquakes, one when Jesus died (27:51) and this one at the tomb. In the Old Testament the earth shakes when God comes down to act (Exodus 19:18; Psalm 18:7).

scene.label: Like lightning, white as snow
scene.text: Daniel saw a heavenly messenger whose face was “like the appearance of lightning” (Daniel 10:6), and the Ancient of Days in a garment “white as snow” (Daniel 7:9). Matthew describes this angel in the same terms.

scene.label: The guards
scene.text: Soldiers who failed in their watch could face severe punishment; Herod later put to death the guards from whom Peter escaped (Acts 12:19). Men trained to stand their ground fell helpless before one messenger from God.

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew tells what happened at the tomb before the women arrived. He has followed the guards since the sealing of the tomb, and here they meet a power no seal could resist. His readers learn how the stone was moved, and that it was not the disciples who moved it.

seeing.reveals: The resurrection was the Father’s act on behalf of His Son. God sent His angel, shook the earth and broke the seal, because, as Peter later preached, “it was not possible that He should be held by it” (Acts 2:24).
seeing.living: Paul prays that believers would know “the exceeding greatness of His power toward us who believe,” the power God “worked in Christ when He raised Him from the dead” (Ephesians 1:19–20). The power that opened this tomb is at work in those who trust Jesus.
seeing.ponder: What would change in your life if you believed that the power that moved this stone is at work in you?

preaching.big_idea: God opened the tomb His enemies had sealed, and its guards became like dead men.
outline: The stone rolled back and sat upon (2b)
preaching.watch_for: Matthew 28 is full of “behold” (vv. 2, 7, 9, 11). Each one calls the reader to look at another surprise of that morning, and the first is the earthquake and the angel.
